Guru Arjan

Stories of the Sikh Gurus

Guru Arjan

The Adi Granth and the Martyrdom

In everyday English — the whole story of the fifth Guru

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the waves of the Amrit Sarovar and the sound of kirtan in the background.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Arjan's calm and sweet, Ram Das's grave, Prithi Chand's bitter.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader, not the listener.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are three kinds of things in this book — Arjan's own bani, written in the Guru Granth Sahib; the stories of the tradition, told in the sangat for centuries; and Emperor Jahangir's own diary, in which he wrote the order for Arjan's death. Where a story comes from the tradition, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where the words are Arjan's own, the book names them.

This book's main story comes from the bani of the Guru Granth Sahib, the traditional life stories, and Jahangir's diary. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Guru Arjan — the heart of this story. Born in Goindwal, the youngest son of Guru Ram Das, the fifth Guru at eighteen, the compiler of the Adi Granth, and the first martyr Guru of the Sikhs.

Guru Ram Das — Arjan's father, the fourth Guru of the Sikhs. First known as Bhai Jetha; he founded Amritsar.

Mata Bhani — Arjan's mother, the daughter of Guru Amar Das.

Prithi Chand — Arjan's eldest brother. He believed the guruship should have been his.

Mahadev — Arjan's middle brother, who lived apart from the world, in devotion.

Mata Ganga — Arjan's wife. Their son was named Hargobind.

Bhai Gurdas — Arjan's trusted Sikh and scholar. It was he who wrote the Adi Granth with his own hand.

Baba Buddha — the oldest and most revered Sikh. He had been in the sangat since Nanak's time; he became the first granthi of the Adi Granth.

Baba Mohan — the son of Guru Amar Das, who held the pothis of the earlier Gurus' bani.

Sai Mian Mir — the Sufi saint of Lahore, of whom the tradition says he laid the foundation stone of the Harmandir Sahib.

Akbar — the emperor of India, in whose reign most of Arjan's work was done.

Jahangir — Akbar's son and successor. It was he who ordered Arjan's arrest.

Khusrau — Jahangir's eldest son, who rebelled against his father.

Chandu Shah — a diwan at the Mughal court, of whom the tradition says he poisoned Jahangir's ear against the Guru.

Guru Hargobind — Arjan's son, who became the sixth Guru at eleven years old.

1 · Birth — Goindwal · · BIRTH — GOINDWAL

On the bank of the Beas river, in Goindwal, a child was born in 1563 — on 15 April 1563. His name was Arjan. His father was Bhai Jetha — who later became known as Guru Ram Das — and his mother was Mata Bhani, the daughter of Guru Amar Das.

Arjan was the youngest son of the house. He had two elder brothers — Prithi Chand, the eldest, and Mahadev, the middle one. The Guru's light lived in the house, but the house was an ordinary Sikh family's home — kirtan in the morning, seva in the day, sangat in the evening.

Arjan was quiet-natured from childhood. He sat beside his father and listened to bani, and even while playing with the sangat's children he hummed kirtan under his breath. Guru Ram Das watched him — this child is not like the others; the flame of the Name is already burning in him.

When Arjan was eleven, his father became Guru — in 1574, after the passing of Guru Amar Das, Bhai Jetha became Guru Ram Das. Now Arjan was the Guru's son — but there was no rank in the house. He and his brothers lived just like the sangat's children.

Arjan began writing bani in childhood itself. He was a poet — his words had a sweetness that touched the listener's heart. People in the sangat said — in this child's bani there is a glimpse of Nanak.

The date of birth — 15 April 1563

Arjan was born on 15 April 1563 in Goindwal — this date is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, and modern scholars agree with it. He was the youngest son of Guru Ram Das and Mata Bhani; Prithi Chand was the eldest brother and Mahadev the middle one.

Pause and think — Arjan was born in the Guru's house — but being born there was not enough to become Guru. What do you think — does a person's family make them great, or their own deeds?

2 · The Succession — The Youngest Son Chosen · · THE SUCCESSION — THE YOUNGEST SON CHOSEN

The year 1581 came. Guru Ram Das's health began to fail. He called his disciples and said — the time has come to hand over the guruship. Everyone in the sangat looked at his sons — at the eldest son, Prithi Chand.

Prithi Chand was sure the guruship was his. He was the eldest, he had been at the court for years, and he believed a son's right belongs to the son. But Guru Ram Das looked at all three of his sons — and chose the youngest, Arjan.

The tradition tells us that Baba Buddha applied the tilak to Arjan's forehead, and Ram Das handed him the guruship. In 1581, at the age of eighteen, Arjan became the fifth Guru of the Sikhs.

Guru Ram Das passed away in 1581. The sangat watched — the Guru had changed, but the light was the same. As one lamp lights another — the flame stays the same, the lamp changes.

But Prithi Chand was not happy with this decision. He said — the guruship was mine, my younger brother snatched it away. He left Amritsar and, with some companions, began building a separate sangat. He began calling himself the Guru — and his followers came to be known as the Minas.

Prithi Chand's opposition lasted all of Arjan's life — and after his martyrdom too. The tradition tells us that he put obstacles in the Guru's work, spread false stories, and carried complaints to the court. But Arjan never answered him with anger. He said — the light the Guru gave cannot be blown out by complaints.

Arjan took up the guruship — and in the same year he was married to Mata Ganga. Some years later, in 1595, their son was born — Hargobind.

Prithi Chand's opposition — tradition and history

Prithi Chand's opposition and his forming a separate sect (the Minas) are recorded in both tradition and history — the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism and modern scholars (Grewal, McLeod) also accept this split. Prithi Chand opposed Hargobind's guruship too, after Arjan's martyrdom. The details of his complaints and schemes come from the tradition's stories — this book's main story only says that the opposition existed, and that it lasted a long time.

Baba Mohan's challenge too

Baba Mohan, the son of Guru Amar Das, also challenged Arjan's authority — this too is recorded in the sources. But his story enters this book only because he held the pothis of the earlier Gurus' bani, which became the foundation of the Adi Granth — that story is in the coming parts.

Pause and think — The guruship went again not to the eldest son, but to the youngest — the one who had proved himself in seva and bani. Do you think a right comes from age — or from worth? And when the opposition comes from inside one's own house, how should it be answered?

3 · The Harmandir Sahib — Four Doors Open to All · · THE HARMANDIR SAHIB — FOUR DOORS OPEN TO ALL

Guru Ram Das had founded Amritsar — and had a pool dug there, the Amrit Sarovar, the Pool of Nectar. Now Arjan thought — in the middle of the pool there should be the Guru's house — a house that everyone can enter.

Arjan began building the Harmandir Sahib — the House of God — in the middle of the sarovar. It was not like other temples. Other temples are built on high ground, so a person must climb up to them. The Harmandir Sahib was built low — below the ground level, in the middle of the pool — so that whoever comes must step down, bow the head, and come in humility.

And the Harmandir Sahib had four doors — one in each direction. That meant — this house is open to everyone. Come from the north or the south, the east or the west — no door is small, no path is closed. Hindu or Muslim, high caste or low — the door is open to all.

The tradition tells us that the first foundation stone of the Harmandir Sahib was laid by the Sufi saint of Lahore, Sai Mian Mir — a Muslim saint's hands laying the foundation of a Sikh temple. That was Arjan's message — God's house belongs to no single religion, it belongs to all.

The work on the Harmandir Sahib was finished by 1604 — the same year the Adi Granth was ready. Amritsar was no longer just a town — it had become the heart of the Sikhs. The sangat began coming from far and wide — and kept coming through all four doors of the Harmandir Sahib.

The pool was named the Amrit Sarovar — the Pool of Nectar. The town took its name from it too — Amritsar. Guru Ram Das had called it Ramdaspur — but on people's tongues the name of the pool won, and the town came to be called Amritsar.

Mian Mir and the foundation stone — the tradition's story

That the first foundation stone of the Harmandir Sahib was laid by Sai Mian Mir is the tradition's story, told in Sikh accounts. No contemporary record of it survives, so history cannot fix it firmly. The foundation is dated to around 1588–89. This book tells it as the tradition's story.

Four doors and a low-built temple — what is certain

The four doors of the Harmandir Sahib, and that it stands in the middle of the sarovar, lower than the surrounding land — these are certain and visible facts. Their meaning — a house open to all, entered by stepping down in humility — is how Sikh tradition explains them.

Pause and think — The Harmandir Sahib has four doors — no door is closed. Which places around you have doors open to everyone — and which places still keep some people outside?

4 · The Adi Granth — The Book of God's Words · · THE ADI GRANTH — THE BOOK OF GOD'S WORDS

Arjan had a great worry before him. The bani of the earlier Gurus — Nanak, Angad, Amar Das and Ram Das — was written in pothis, but those pothis lay scattered here and there. Some people were mixing in their own words and handing them out — Prithi Chand too. Arjan thought — if no true book of the bani is made, how will the true word reach the generations to come?

Arjan decided — a firm book of the bani will be made. The bani of the earlier Gurus, his own bani, and the bani of those bhagats in whose words God's truth lived — all in a single book.

The pothis of the earlier Gurus' bani were with Baba Mohan — the son of Guru Amar Das. He was not ready to give them. The story tells us that Arjan did not press him — he sang the bani, with humility, and won Mohan's heart — and the pothis were given.

Arjan sent his companions across India — to gather the bani of the bhagats. The bani of Kabir, the bani of Farid, the bani of Ravidas, the bani of Namdev — Hindu bhagat, Muslim Sufi, high caste, low caste — Arjan asked no one their religion or caste. He asked only one thing — does God's truth live in this word?

Then, in Amritsar, near Ramsar — beside a small pool — the work began. Arjan spoke the bani, and Bhai Gurdas wrote it down with his own hand. Gurdas was a scholar, Arjan's trusted Sikh — and he put none of his own bani in the book. When Arjan said — give your bani too — Gurdas said — my bani is not equal to this book. Arjan blessed him and said — your bani will be the key to this book.

The book was arranged by raag — each word in its own raga, as it is sung in kirtan. Arjan's own bani was the largest part of it — 2,218 shabads. The bani of the four earlier Gurus, the bani of fifteen bhagats, and the bani of eleven bhatts also came into it.

The book was completed on 29 August 1604. And on 1 September 1604 it was installed in the Harmandir Sahib — on a manji, on a high seat, with a chaur beside it. Baba Buddha became its first granthi. And Arjan bowed his head before the book — and sat lower than it. The book was above, the Guru below.

From that day the book was called the Adi Granth — the First Book. A hundred years later, Guru Gobind Singh added Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani to it — and it became the Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal Guru of the Sikhs.

In this same time Arjan also wrote his most beloved composition — Sukhmani Sahib, the song of peace. Written at Ramsar, this bani is read in every Sikh home even today. Its first line is —

Sukhmani sukh amrit Prabh naam.

It means — Sukhmani, the nectar of peace, is the Name of God.

The dates of the Adi Granth — certain facts

The completion of the Adi Granth on 29 August 1604 and its installation in the Harmandir Sahib on 1 September 1604 are accepted in both Sikh tradition and modern scholarship. That Bhai Gurdas was the scribe, Baba Buddha the first granthi, and the work was done at Ramsar, Amritsar — these too are firmly held.

Whose bani, how much bani

The Adi Granth holds the bani of the first four Gurus, Arjan's own bani of 2,218 shabads, the bani of fifteen bhagats (Kabir, Farid, Ravidas, Namdev, Jaidev, Trilochan, Parmanand, Sadhna, Ramanand, Beni, Dhanna, Pipa, Sain, Surdas, Bhikhan) and the bani of eleven bhatts. Arjan chose only the words in which God's truth lived — and he rejected some words too.

The pothis from Baba Mohan — the tradition's story

The story of receiving the pothis from Baba Mohan — that Arjan won his heart by singing bani — is the tradition's story. It is certain that the pothis were with Mohan and that Arjan received them; the manner of receiving is what the tradition tells.

Sukhmani Sahib — at Ramsar

Sukhmani Sahib is Arjan's composition, written according to tradition at Ramsar, Amritsar — around 1602–03. It is a long bani of twenty-four ashtpadis, and it stands in the Guru Granth Sahib today.

Pause and think — Arjan put the bani of Hindu bhagats in his book, and of a Muslim Sufi too — and he did not place his own bani above theirs, he put them all in one book. Do you think truth lives in only one religion — or can it be found everywhere?

5 · The Growing Sangat and the Emperor's Eye · · THE GROWING SANGAT AND THE EMPEROR'S EYE

In Arjan's time the sangat grew fast. People began coming to Amritsar — from Punjab, from Delhi, from far away. Kirtan sounded in the Harmandir Sahib, the langar ran, and in the sangat there were Hindus and Muslims too — all chanting the one Name.

Arjan also made the running of the sangat firm. Guru Ram Das had begun the masand system — trusted Sikhs in far-off sangats, who spread the Guru's message and carried the sangat's offerings to the Guru. Arjan strengthened it further, and told the sangat — if you can, give a tenth part of your earnings — dasvandh — for the Guru's work.

Arjan founded more towns around Amritsar too — Tarn Taran, where a great sarovar was built, and Kartarpur, in the Jalandhar Doab. The sangat was no longer in one place — it had spread across all of Punjab.

In Arjan's time the langar ran as before — Guru Nanak had begun it, Amar Das had made it the condition for meeting the Guru, and Arjan made it greater still. Beside the Harmandir Sahib the langar stayed open day and night — whoever came was fed, whoever they were.

But the more the sangat grew, the sharper the court's gaze became. In Delhi sat Emperor Akbar — he had mostly left the Sikhs alone. But there were people in his court — Hindu pandits and Muslim ulema too — who could not bear that one Guru had so great a sangat, in which Hindus came and Muslims came.

They filled Akbar's ears — this Guru is drawing Hindus away from their own faith, and Muslims too. His book speaks of the Hindu faith and of Islam too — this book belittles both religions. Akbar paid little attention to these words. But in 1605 Akbar died — and his son Jahangir sat on the throne.

Jahangir was not like his father. He was suspicious, and he disliked whatever lay outside his control. He wrote in his diary — at Goindwal there lives a Hindu, Arjan, whom people call Guru. He has drawn simple-minded Hindus after him — and some ignorant Muslims too. For a long time I have wanted to close his shop, or bring him into Islam.

Jahangir needed only one chance. And that chance came from his own house — from the rebellion of his eldest son, Khusrau.

Masands and dasvandh — certain facts

The masand system was begun by Guru Ram Das and strengthened by Arjan; dasvandh — a tenth of one's earnings — also belongs to Arjan's time. Both are recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism and by modern scholars (Grewal, McLeod). Tarn Taran and Kartarpur (Jalandhar Doab) were also founded in Arjan's time.

Jahangir's diary — his own words

Emperor Jahangir wrote in his diary, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, that Arjan lived at Goindwal, that people called him Guru, that he had drawn Hindus and some Muslims after him, and that Jahangir had long wanted to close his 'shop'. These are Jahangir's own words — this book gives them as such.

Pause and think — Arjan forced no one to become a Sikh — people came of their own accord. Yet the court found it dangerous. Do you think that when people are drawn of their own accord to something good, it should be stopped?

6 · Jahangir and Khusrau's Rebellion · · JAHANGIR AND KHUSRAU'S REBELLION

The year 1606 came. Jahangir's eldest son, Khusrau, rebelled against his father. Khusrau believed the throne was his by right — Akbar had loved him more too. He fled from Agra and went towards Punjab — where he hoped to find supporters.

Fleeing, Khusrau came to Goindwal — to Guru Arjan. Jahangir wrote in his diary that Khusrau stopped at the Guru's place, and the Guru marked his forehead with a tilak — as if giving him a blessing.

The tradition tells us that Arjan gave Khusrau not only a blessing — he also gave him some rupees, so that he could continue his journey. The tradition also tells us that Arjan gave Khusrau no weapons and no soldiers — only the help he would give any hungry, thirsty traveller.

But for Jahangir that was enough. His diary says — Khusrau went to the Guru, the Guru marked his forehead with a tilak, and this is proof that the Guru is with the rebel. Jahangir ordered — Arjan's property shall be seized, and he shall be handed over for punishment.

Khusrau's rebellion was soon crushed — he was caught, blinded, and later killed. But Jahangir's anger stayed on Arjan. He had found the chance he had waited years for.

The tilak — Jahangir's diary and the tradition

That Khusrau's forehead was marked with a tilak is written in Jahangir's own diary (Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri) — in his eyes it was the proof against Arjan. The gift of rupees is the tradition's story. It is also the tradition that says Arjan gave Khusrau no weapons or soldiers — only a traveller's help.

Khusrau's end

Khusrau's rebellion was crushed in 1606 — he was caught, blinded, and later died. This is a firm fact of history.

Pause and think — Arjan helped a fleeing man — as he would help any hungry traveller. Can helping be wrong — if the man is someone's enemy? And should a Guru look at who is asking for help before helping?

7 · The Arrest and the Martyrdom — Lahore · · THE ARREST AND THE MARTYRDOM — LAHORE

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

Jahangir's order came — Guru Arjan was to be arrested and brought to Lahore. Soldiers came to Amritsar and took the Guru away. There was uproar in the sangat — why is the Guru being taken away? Arjan told the sangat — do not be afraid. Whatever happens, happens by God's will.

In Lahore a fine was laid on the Guru — two lakh rupees, and an order to seize his property. Jahangir's diary says the Guru was handed over for punishment. Arjan refused to pay the fine — he said, I have done no wrong.

The tradition tells us that after this the Guru was put through five days of torture — he was made to sit on a hot plate, and hot sand was poured over him. The tradition also tells us that Sai Mian Mir wished to save the Guru by speaking to Jahangir — but Arjan refused. He said — this is God's will, let it be so.

The tradition tells us that on the fifth day the Guru was taken to the Ravi river for a bath — and he went into the river, and never came back. His body was given to the Ravi. In Lahore, near the fort, that place stands even today — Gurdwara Dera Sahib.

In Arjan's own bani there is a line, which he may have written for just such a time —

Tera bhana meetha laage.

It means — Your will, Your pleasure, tastes sweet to me.

Guru Arjan's martyrdom took place on 30 May 1606 — at the age of forty-three. He became the first martyr Guru of the Sikhs — and his martyrdom changed the very direction of the Sikh panth.

The certain part of the martyrdom — what is proven

The certain part is this — Arjan was arrested on Jahangir's orders, a fine was laid on him in Lahore, and he died in custody in Lahore in 1606. Jahangir's own diary (Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri) records the order for arrest and punishment. The date of death is held to be 30 May 1606. This is the part history accepts.

The details of the torture — the tradition's story

Sitting on a hot plate and hot sand being poured, five days of torture, and Sai Mian Mir coming to save him — all of this is the tradition's story, told in Gurbilas literature. Jahangir's diary gives no detail of torture — and outside witnesses say different things too. So this book tells the torture only as the tradition's story, without detail, in one place — and there is no picture in this part.

Outside witnesses — Xavier and the Dabistan

The Jesuit priest Father Jerome Xavier, present at the Mughal court in Lahore, wrote to Goa on 25 September 1606 that the Guru had been arrested, Hindus tried to free him by paying the fine, and when the money did not come he was given such ill-usage that he died. The Persian book Dabistan-i-Mazahib (written about forty years later) says a fine was laid on the Guru, he could not pay it, and he died outside Lahore in the sun and heat, of his wounds. Both witnesses accept the death — but they differ on its details.

Chandu Shah — the tradition's story

Chandu Shah's (Diwan Chandu Lal's) role — that he poisoned Jahangir's ear and had the Guru tortured, because Arjan had refused his daughter's marriage proposal for Hargobind — is the tradition's story, found in writings from the eighteenth century onwards. No contemporary record of it survives. So this book names Chandu Shah only in this note, as the tradition's story — not in the main story.

Pause and think — Arjan said — Tera bhana meetha laage. Do you think it is possible, even in hard times, to call God's will sweet? And does martyrdom mean defeat — or something else?

8 · The Light Passes to Hargobind — From Rosary to Sword · · THE LIGHT PASSES TO HARGOBIND — FROM ROSARY TO SWORD

After Arjan's martyrdom there was silence in the sangat. The Guru had gone — and behind him remained his son Hargobind, only eleven years old. The sangat wondered — what will happen now? Will the panth come to an end?

But Arjan had thought of everything before he went. He called Hargobind and said — son, now it is your turn. But this time the guruship will not be as before. Now the sangat needs not only the rosary — it needs the sword too.

The tradition tells us that Hargobind wore two swords — one Miri, the sword of kingship, and one Piri, the sword of sainthood. One sword to protect the world, the other to protect the faith. The Guru would no longer be only a saint — he would be a saint-soldier.

Hargobind also built the Akal Takht in Amritsar — a high throne before the Harmandir Sahib, from where the Guru would give decisions in worldly matters. The Harmandir Sahib was God's house — the Akal Takht became the house of the Guru's decisions.

Hargobind told the sangat — from now on, when you bring offerings, bring horses and arms too. The sangat heard — and understood. The Guru's light was now burning in a new form — the same flame, a new lamp.

Arjan's martyrdom had changed the Sikh panth. Before, the Gurus ran the panth in peace, with seva and bani. Now the panth had to protect itself too. This turn began with Arjan's martyrdom — and Hargobind carried it forward.

Two swords and the Akal Takht — tradition and history

Hargobind wearing two swords — Miri and Piri — and building the Akal Takht are held as firm facts in Sikh tradition, and modern scholars also count them among the great events of Hargobind's time. The Akal Takht was built in 1606, after the martyrdom. Arjan's last words to Hargobind are the tradition's story, told in Gurbilas literature.

Pause and think — Arjan was a Guru of the rosary — and his son also took up the sword. Do you think peace ever needs the sword? And can one man be both a saint and a soldier?

To Think About · · TO THINK ABOUT

Arjan's story is not the story of a king, nor of a warrior. It is the story of a man who became Guru at eighteen, who made a book of God's words, who built a house open to all — and who then gave his life at forty-three.

His message fits in three words — Naam, Daan, Ishnaan. Chant the Name, share what you eat, and keep the mind pure. Arjan did not only say this message — he wrote it in a book, built it into a house, and lived it with his life.

Arjan taught that a book is not only paper — a book can be a Guru. He seated the Adi Granth above himself — and said, from now on the Word itself is the Guru. A hundred years later, when Guru Gobind Singh placed the light in the Granth, it was Arjan's own dream fulfilled.

And the greatest thing — Arjan said that God's house belongs to all. The four doors of the Harmandir Sahib stand open even today — and in the Adi Granth there is Kabir's bani, and Farid's, and Ravidas's. Whoever seeks the truth may find it in any faith, in any caste.

Arjan's own bani stands in the Guru Granth Sahib even today — 2,218 shabads. The most beloved among them is Sukhmani Sahib — the song of peace, read in every Sikh home.

After Arjan came five more Gurus — Hargobind, Har Rai, Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur, and Gobind Singh. And in the end the light passed into the Guru Granth Sahib — which is the Guru of the Sikhs even today. Their stories will come in the next books of this series.

But this fifth book ends here — in Amritsar, on the bank of the sarovar, with a question — if Arjan were here today, what would he say in your house, in your city? Perhaps just this — chant the Name, share what you eat, and keep the door open to all.

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source — Arjan's own bani

This book's firmest foundation is Guru Arjan's own bani, recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib — 2,218 shabads. The greatest among them is Sukhmani Sahib — a bani of twenty-four ashtpadis, written at Ramsar. Where this book says 'Arjan's own bani', this is its basis.

The Adi Granth — 1604

The completion of the Adi Granth (29 August 1604), its installation in the Harmandir Sahib (1 September 1604), Bhai Gurdas as its scribe and Baba Buddha as its first granthi — these are held firm in both Sikh tradition and modern scholarship. The Adi Granth also holds the bani of fifteen bhagats and eleven bhatts.

Jahangir's diary — the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri

Emperor Jahangir wrote in his diary, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, that Arjan lived at Goindwal, people called him Guru, he had drawn Hindus and some Muslims after him, Khusrau stopped with him and he marked Khusrau's forehead with a tilak, and Jahangir ordered his property seized and him handed over for punishment. This is this book's strongest contemporary source — and the certain part of the martyrdom rests on it.

Outside witnesses — Xavier and the Dabistan

The Jesuit priest Father Jerome Xavier's letter of 25 September 1606 (to Goa) and the Persian book Dabistan-i-Mazahib (written about forty years later) — both accept Arjan's arrest, fine and death in custody, but they differ on its details. Their full account is in the notes of the martyrdom part.

The traditional life stories — Janamsakhi and Gurbilas

The stories of Arjan's life are found in the Janamsakhis and Gurbilas literature. They were written decades and centuries after Arjan's death, and history and tradition are mixed in them. Every story from the tradition in this book is told as 'the tradition tells us' and made clear in its own note — above all the details of the torture, the Mian Mir foundation stone, and Chandu Shah's role.

Modern scholarship

The dates and events in this book were checked against the work of modern scholars — J.S. Grewal, 'The Sikhs of the Punjab'; W.H. McLeod, 'The Sikhs — History, Religion and Society'; and the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala). Where scholars and tradition say different things, this book records both.

One clear thing

This book does not show Arjan against any religion. He gave the bani of Hindu bhagats and Muslim Sufis a place in his book — and his message was not to divide, but to join. His martyrdom was not against any religion either — it came by the order of an emperor who feared his growing sangat.

The End · · THE END

The story is over — but Arjan's bani is not over yet.

In the next book — Guru Hargobind, who wore two swords and built the Akal Takht.

Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh.
